findings.title: User label and creation time are lost when recovery codes are created in user storage
findings.body: createRecoveryCodesCredential() builds the UserCredentialModel passed to user.credentialManager().updateCredential() from only the raw generatedCodes list (`new UserCredentialModel("", credentialModel.getType(), recoveryCodesJson)`). The RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel passed in (which carries the userLabel entered by the user in RecoveryAuthnCodesAction and the original generatedAt timestamp) is only used in the local-storage fallback branch (`recoveryCodeCredentialProvider.createCredential(...)`). When the credential is actually created in a user storage provider (the success path), the userLabel and createdAt metadata are silently dropped – the storage provider only ever receives the raw code list. Any UserStorageProvider implementation that tries to preserve the user-chosen label (as the updated BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage.getCredentials() attempts to read back via getUserLabel()) will always get null, so the recovery-codes label feature is effectively broken for storage-backed users.

findings.title: Recovery-codes provider id is now a magic string instead of a constant
findings.body: createRecoveryCodesCredential() looks up the provider with the hard-coded literal "keycloak-recovery-authn-codes" instead of using RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialProviderFactory.PROVIDER_ID (whose import was removed from RecoveryAuthnCodesAction.java in this same PR). If the provider id ever changes, this string will silently diverge from the real constant and the fallback-to-local-storage path will fail without a compile error to catch it.

findings.title: Recovery codes are stored and validated in plaintext with no single-use enforcement
findings.body: updateCredential() stores the raw challengeResponse (the JSON array of plaintext recovery codes) directly into CredentialModel.credentialData, and isValid() simply checks `generatedKeys.stream().anyMatch(key -> key.equals(input.getChallengeResponse()))`. There is no hashing step (unlike passwords, which go through PasswordHashProvider) and no mechanism to mark a matched code as used/remove it from the stored list, so the same recovery code can be reused indefinitely once validated. Since this file is the reference/compatibility example for implementing recovery codes in custom user storage providers, it demonstrates an insecure pattern that defeats the single-use guarantee that recovery codes are supposed to provide; no test in this PR exercises reuse of an already-used code to catch this.

findings.title: getCredentials() does not null-check myUser, unlike sibling methods
findings.body: The new getCredentials(RealmModel, UserModel) override calls `var myUser = getMyUser(user);` and then directly dereferences `myUser.recoveryCodes` / passes myUser to credentialModels.add(myUser.getOtp()), without checking for null. Other methods in this class (isConfiguredFor, getDisableableCredentialTypesStream) explicitly guard against `myUser == null`. If this method is ever invoked for a user not present in the in-memory map, it will throw a NullPointerException instead of failing gracefully like the other methods.

findings.title: New test does not verify recovery-code single-use behavior or label persistence
findings.body: testRecoveryKeysSetupAndLogin() only exercises generating recovery codes in the user-storage provider and logging in once with one code; it never attempts to reuse the same code a second time (which should fail) and never sets/verifies a user label for the generated credential. Given that the credential metadata handling (userLabel/createdAt) and single-use enforcement are both affected by this change, the added test does not catch either regression.
